authors: Caves EM, Fernández-Juricic E, Kelley LA
title: Ecological and morphological correlates of visual acuity in birds (supplementary Table S1)
why: The main text was read; its supplementary Table S1 lists the acuity of each of 94 bird species, which would set the sharpness of the hawk, owl, duck, wader and bird views from named species instead of order means.

authors: Potier S, Mitkus M, Kelber A
title: Visual adaptations of diurnal and nocturnal raptors
journal: Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology
why: A review of raptor and owl vision whose tables would give acuity, flicker fusion and fovea data for the hawk and owl views.

authors: Höglund J, Mitkus M, Olsson P, Lind O, Drews A, Bloch NI, Kelber A, Strandh M
title: Owls lack UV-sensitive cone opsin and red oil droplets, but see UV light at night: Retinal transcriptomes and ocular media transmittance
why: Would settle which cone types owls keep, whether their oil droplets are coloured, and how much ultraviolet their eyes pass, which sets the owl view's colour.

title: Anatomical and behavioral correlates of visual acuity in the great horned owl
why: Acuity of the great horned owl, the second most recorded owl in Alachua, measured behaviourally and anatomically.

title: Visual acuity in the tawny owl (Strix aluco)
why: Acuity of the tawny owl, the closest measured relative of the barred owl, Alachua's most recorded owl.

title: Total panoramic vision in the mallard duck, Anas platyrhynchos
why: Gives the mallard's full visual field, the basis of the duck view's 360-degree picture.

authors: Potier S, Bonadonna F, Kelber A, Martin GR, Isard PF, Dulaurent T, Duriez O
title: Visual abilities in two raptors with different ecology
why: Acuity values and visual fields for the Harris's hawk and black kite, the only accipitrids with both measured; would set the hawk view's sharpness.

title: The visual acuity and refractive state of the American kestrel (Falco sparverius)
why: Behavioural acuity of the American kestrel, the commonest small falcon in North America, to check the 160 cycles per degree reported for a falcon in 1976.

title: Assessment of visual acuity and contrast sensitivity in the chick using an optokinetic nystagmus paradigm
why: Acuity and contrast sensitivity of the chicken, which would set the sharpness of the wader view for gamebirds.

title: Animal Eyes, second edition: chapter 5, Lens eyes on land (pp. 94-128), and chapter 9, Movements of the eyes (pp. 215-241, head-bobbing in birds p. 227)
why: The Drive copy came through only to p. 65; these chapters treat bird eyes, deep foveae and head-bobbing, and would check the hawk and wader pictures.

authors: Lisney TJ, Rubene D, Rózsa J, Løvlie H, Håstad O, Ödeen A
title: Behavioural assessment of flicker fusion frequency in chicken Gallus gallus domesticus
why: The primary measurement of chicken flicker fusion (87 Hz as cited), to confirm the wader view's pace.

authors: Potier S, Duriez O, Cunningham GB, Bonhomme V, O'Rourke CT, Fernández-Juricic E, Bonadonna F
title: Visual field shape and foraging ecology in diurnal raptors
why: Visual fields of 15 accipitriform raptors, which would give the field and blind areas of buteos, kites and eagles.

title: The Deep Fovea, Sideways Vision and Spiral Flight Paths in Raptors
why: The full text gives the angles of the deep and shallow foveae per species, needed to place the two sharp spots in the hawk view.

authors: Mitkus M, Olsson P, Toomey MB, Corbo JC, Kelber A
title: Specialized photoreceptor composition in the raptor fovea
why: Photoreceptor make-up of the central and temporal foveae, to decide whether the hawk view's sharp spots carry full colour.

authors: Dyson ML, Klump GM, Gauger B
title: Absolute hearing thresholds and critical masking ratios in the European barn owl: a comparison with other owls
why: Barn owl audiogram and the best frequency of hearing, for the owl hearing row and its microphone effect.

title: Absolute visual threshold and scotopic spectral sensitivity in the tawny owl Strix aluco
why: The tawny owl's absolute visual threshold, which would set how far the owl view brightens dim scenes.

title: The visual fields of the tawny owl, Strix aluco L
why: The full visual field of the tawny owl, including the blind area above and behind the head.

authors: Porter ML, Kingston AC, McCready R, Cameron EG, Hofmann CM, Suarez L, Olsen GH, Cronin TW, Robinson PR
title: Characterization of visual pigments, oil droplets, lens and cornea in the whooping crane Grus americana
why: Visual pigments, oil droplets and eye media of the whooping crane, the only crane measured, for the sandhill crane in the wader view.

authors: Lisney TJ, Stecyk K, Kolominsky J, Graves GR, Wylie DRW, Iwaniuk AN
title: Comparison of eye morphology and retinal topography in two species of new world vultures (Aves: Cathartidae)
why: Retinal topography and anatomical acuity of turkey and black vultures, which would decide whether New World vultures need a view of their own.

title: The retinal binocular field of the pigeon (Columba livia: English racing homer)
why: The pigeon's binocular field, to replace the operational field used in the wader view.

title: Head bobbing and the movement of the centre of gravity in walking pigeons (Columba livia)
why: Timing of the hold and thrust phases in walking pigeons, which would replace the invented hold length in the wader view.

title: Retinal Ganglion Cell Topography of Five Species of Ground-Foraging Birds
why: Gives the anatomical acuity of the mourning dove and four ground-foraging songbirds, the commonest dove and several common songbirds.

title: The eye of a passeriform bird, the European starling (Sturnus vulgaris): eye movement amplitude, visual fields and schematic optics
why: The starling's eye movements and visual field, a typical songbird's field for the bird view.

authors: Solov’yov IA, Mouritsen H, Schulten K
title: Acuity of a Cryptochrome and Vision-Based Magnetoreception System in Birds
why: Models what a cryptochrome compass in the retina might add to the visual scene, the nearest evidence for the invented magnetic shading.

title: Visual fields in woodcocks Scolopax rusticola (Scolopacidae; Charadriiformes)
why: The woodcock's visual field, the clearest case of panoramic vision in shorebirds.

title: Spatial visual acuity of the eagle Aquila audax: a behavioural, optical and anatomical investigation
why: Primary source of the wedge-tailed eagle's acuity, to confirm 138 to 143 cycles per degree.

title: Complex Distribution of Avian Color Vision Systems Revealed by Sequencing the SWS1 Opsin from Total DNA
why: The species table behind the violet and ultraviolet classes of crows, jays and tyrant flycatchers.

authors: Knudsen EI, Blasdel GG, Konishi M
title: Sound localization by the barn owl (Tyto alba) measured with the search coil technique
why: Barn owl sound localization measured with head movements.

authors: Fernández-Juricic E, Gall MD, Dolan T, Tisdale V, Martin GR
title: The visual fields of two ground‐foraging birds, House Finches and House Sparrows, allow for simultaneous foraging and anti‐predator vigilance
why: Visual fields of house finches and house sparrows, two commonly photographed songbirds.

authors: Lind O, Mitkus M, Olsson P, Kelber A
title: Ultraviolet sensitivity and colour vision in raptor foraging
why: Ocular media transmission values for buzzards, sparrowhawks, red kites and kestrels.
